raw_case_text:
We report the case of a 40-year-old female patient, married, currently unemployed but with an occupational history of working at a gas station, who presented to the clinic reporting sleeplessness over the past two years.
She reported not sleeping at all during most nights. On the nights she perceived to sleep, she would fall asleep around 4:00 a.m. only, and just for a few minutes. Her usual bedtime was 10:00 p.m. and she got up around 9:00 a.m.
The patient informed irritability and recurring negative thoughts worried her all night. She reported excessive daytime sleepiness, but the Epworth Sleepiness Scale score was zero. The patient denied napping during the day, nightmares, snoring, restless leg syndrome symptoms, or other sleep complaints before these last two years.
The patient had a history of acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS, or stage IV HIV infection, according to the World Health Organization) that had been diagnosed 13 years previously, during a prenatal care visit. Treatment with an antiretroviral therapy was initiated, but the adhesion to treatment was extremely poor; over the past 2 years, total CD4 count ranged from 15 to 85/microl and HIV-RNA count from 10,560 to 24,343 copies/ml. She also had a previous history of appendectomy with ileostomy, with subsequent diagnosis of diffuse malignant B-cell lymphoma, from which she received appropriate care and is on follow-up. Two years ago, she began episodes of a progressive headache and dizziness. A computed tomography (CT) scan of the brain during the investigation revealed an extensive area of hypodensity in the left nucleocapsular region, showing lesion in ring enhancement in the region with surrounding perilesional edema after contrast administration. A magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain acquired afterward showed a residual lesion in the left nucleocapsular region (Figure 1). Sulfadiazine, pyrimethamine, folinic acid and dexamethasone were used to treat neurotoxoplasmosis, along with the antiretroviral therapy, with good outcomes.
The patient was referred to the sleep disorders clinic with the complaint of total insomnia. The initial treatment included amitriptyline and trazodone, with no response. The neurological examination was then normal, and no cognitive disorder was identified. A polysomnography showed a sleep efficiency of 74,2%, and total sleep time of 290 minutes (16.4% N1, 36.9% N2, 27.6% N3 and 19.1% REM), 16.6 arousals per hour, waketime after sleep onset of 97.5 minutes, normal apnea-hypopnea index (1.0/h), a nadir SaO2 97% and no indication of periodic limb movements in sleep index of 1.4/h.
The patient, however, reported not being able to sleep at any time during the exam, leading to the diagnosis of SSM. She received the orientation about the disorder and on sleep hygiene and cognitive behavior therapy was recommended.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 40-year-old married, unemployed woman with longstanding poorly controlled AIDS and prior treated cerebral toxoplasmosis presented to the sleep disorders clinic with a 2-year history of perceived complete nightly sleeplessness.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Over the preceding 2 years—beginning around the time she was treated for left nucleocapsular cerebral toxoplasmosis—the patient reported not sleeping at all on most nights, or falling asleep only around 4:00 a.m. for a few minutes despite a bedtime of 10:00 p.m. and wake time of 9:00 a.m., accompanied by nocturnal worry and irritability. Trials of amitriptyline and trazodone failed to improve her perceived insomnia.
subjective.past_medical_history: WHO Stage IV HIV/AIDS diagnosed 13 years prior during prenatal care with chronic poor adherence to antiretroviral therapy; prior appendectomy with ileostomy and treated diffuse malignant B-cell lymphoma; left nucleocapsular cerebral toxoplasmosis 2 years prior (successfully treated with sulfadiazine, pyrimethamine, folinic acid, and dexamethasone). Former gas station attendant.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for perceived total insomnia, nocturnal rumination, irritability, and subjective daytime fatigue (Epworth Sleepiness Scale score = 0); negative for daytime napping, nightmares, snoring, or restless legs syndrome.

objective.physical_examination: Neurological and cognitive examinations were completely normal; Epworth Sleepiness Scale score was 0.
objective.advanced_workup: Over the preceding 2 years, CD4+ T-cell counts ranged from 15 to 85 cells/µL. Prior brain CT and follow-up brain MRI demonstrated a residual treated lesion in the left nucleocapsular (basal ganglia/internal capsule) region. Overnight in-laboratory polysomnography (PSG)—during which the patient subjectively claimed she had not slept at all—demonstrated an objective total sleep time of 290 minutes (4.8 hours) and sleep efficiency of 74.2% (16.4% stage N1, 36.9% stage N2, 27.6% stage N3, and 19.1% REM sleep), wake after sleep onset of 97.5 minutes, 16.6 arousals/hour, a normal apnea-hypopnea index (1.0/hour, nadir SpO2 97%), and a normal periodic limb movement index (1.4/hour).

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Sleep state misperception (SSM / paradoxical insomnia) potentially related to left nucleocapsular post-toxoplasmosis basal ganglia injury in a 40-year-old woman with poorly controlled WHO Stage IV HIV/AIDS (CD4+ count 15–85 cells/µL, plasma HIV-RNA 10,560–24,343 copies/mL). Confirmed by the striking discrepancy between her subjective perception of zero sleep during overnight monitoring and objective polysomnography recording 290 minutes of preserved N1–N3 and REM sleep architecture (74.2% sleep efficiency) without sleep apnea or periodic limb movements. Managed with patient education/reassurance regarding sleep state misperception, sleep hygiene counseling, and referral for cognitive-behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I).
